I see a lot of cries to "Defund the Police." I would ask that you dont give in to a vocal few and follow this foolish course of action. improve training, resources, and oversight, but dont defund. The Washington Post publised a story noting that in 2015 the were over 50 million interactions between police and the public. .00002 percent resulted in a police shooting. that shows there is room to improve, but NOT a widespread problem. Please use prudence and good judgment and dont get swept up in the moment. Dont defund the police.

I understand there is a lot of anger right now, but I do not think defunding or even a hiring freeze is the right answer. Please take the time and do it right instead of trying to rush something in at the last minute that could do more harm than good to our beautiful city.

I do not agree that we should rush to defund (re-allocate SLCPD funds). The city, council, and citizens should work together with Chief Brown to make adjustments to policy and have civil discussions about our concerns. The SLCPD has been more responsive to the public's concerns than departments in other American cities and we would be doing them a great disservice by lumping them in with 'bad cops' and 'bad departments.' I don't think police departments need surplus military vehicles and equi'ment however so perhaps just be clear on what the department funds should be used for....recruiting and paying high-quality candidates, training, community programs where the police can work together with the community. A rush to judgement and knee-jerk reaction will only harm our city in the short and long-term. Please re-consider this rush to re-allocate police funding and work with the SLCPD to continue to improve.

I am a 74-year-old white male resident of Salt Lake City. I am in solidarity with the ongoing peaceful protests against the mistreatment of minorities through policing and more generally through institutionally entrenched raci'm. I have not been marching because of Covid-19 concerns. I have been watching nationwide protests and listening to black leaders, police chiefs, and thoughtful commentators. In Utah the problems with raci'm extend to the treatment of not just African-Americans, but Hispanics, Pacific Islanders, and Native Americans. For the moment we are focusing on police. We need a new community-focused model of public safety so that police are viewed by all communities as allies and not oppressors. See, for example, how this works in Camden, New Jersey. 1. Locate police in communities so they get to know residents and earn their trust. 2. Demilitarize police -- no more military-grade weapons. 3. Abolish no-knock tactics. 4. Make it a policy: no shooting of fleeing suspects unless they pose an I'mediate threat to the lives of others. 5. Step up de-escalation training. 6. Abolish training sessions that instill a "predator culture" in police. 7. Strengthen civilian review and make reviews of misconduct transparent. 8. Police are not trained to do social work, and we shouldn't be expecting them to serve that role. In too many situations the homeless and poor need community help, not law enforcement. Hire social workers to replace them. 9. Reward good police behavior with pay increases. Most of thereforms on this list amount to re'venting public safety and require a long-term effort. But with the current budget deliberations, there is an opportunity to start making somereforms right away. Please reduce the budget for our police force and increase funding for social work and community services.

I am a resident of District 4. I am writing to demand that the City Council adopt a People's Budget that prioritizes community wellbeing and redirects funding away from the police. We are in the midst of widespread upheaval over the systemic violence of policing, embodied by the SLCPD's well documented history of murdering Black people. We will no longer accept empty gestures and suggestions of reform.? We are demanding that our voices be heard now, and that real change be made to the way this city allocates its resources. Support for communities in need is necessary now, more than ever. But instead, the Mayor has proposed an increase in funding to the SLCPD, despite the fact that crime has fallen considerably during the past few months. The SLCPD has seen a rise in overtime pay which, more often than not, is paid out to officers responsible for harassing the unhoused, and Black, Indigenous, people of color. We demand that the City Council defund the SLCPD. We join the calls of those across the country to #DefundThePolice. We demand a budget that adequately and effectively meets the needs of at-risk Utahns during this trying and uncertain time, when livelihoods are on the line. We demand a budget that supports community wellbeing, rather than empowers the police forces that tear them apart. Although City Council has avoided voting or revising Mayor Mendenhall's draconian budget proposal, the document is back in your hands. It is your duty to represent your constituents. I am urging you to completely revise the SLC budget for 2020-2021 fiscal year, and to fund #CareNotCops. You need to adopt a People's Budget. Public opinion is with me. Thank you for your time, Faafota Mulitalo Rasmussen Sent from my iPhone

I apologize for the second email but I would also like you to take a look at the Justice in Policing Act of 2020 that was just introduced. No where does it mandate defunding of Police across the U.S. The majority of the act requires strict protocols in utilizing body and dash cameras, it calls for further training, bans certain uses of force, most of which the Salt Lake City Police Department has already implemented. However, if there is further training that is required this cannot be provided without the budget. The Act also calls for more accountability, control, monitoring, and reporting of the Police Department. From: Ferevski, Edwin Sent: Tuesday, June 9, 2020 9:33 AM To: Rogers, James ; Johnston, Andrew ; Wharton, Chris ; Valdemoros, Ana ; Mano, Darin ; Dugan, Dan ; Fowler, Amy ; Mendenhall, Erin Subject: Police Budget City Council Members, It is an honor to address you all. I am writing this email in response to your proposed budget cut of the Salt Lake City Police Department. I don't want to take up too much of your time but I want to bring some points into perspective. First, I do not care what you decide on if it would solely affect ME. I will continue to serve our great city, a city that I was raised in, no matter how unequipped, underfunded, or unsupported I am ? that is what I promised to do. However, I cannot speak for the rest of my brothers and sisters who are all a part of this Department with me. I cannot speak for the Officers, the Office Technicians, the Crime Scene Technicians, Evidence Technicians, the Case Workers, Mental Health Therapists, Social Workers, Information Specialists, Accountants, Records Technicians, and so many more. What I want you to notice is that just one of those positions mentioned is a sworn position; the remainder are Civilians who you would be taking from. Not only that, but those Civilian employees provide a vital role to our Police Department with due regard to Homeless Outreach, Mental Health, Crime Statistics, Training, Organization, I could go on. What is the most troubling to me is that I bel!ved wholeheartedly that these recent events would show how underfunded our Police Department already is. Our agency had to call outside Police Departments for assistance on Saturday May 30th. We could not have accomplished what we did that day without them and they have been with us every day ever since the initial protest. Our Public Order Unit, which I am not a part of, has been asking the Department and City for more funding for over a year now. I stood next to those men and women, half of whom were underequipped; who did not have a full kit, a shield, or a face helmet while others did. About a month ago my patrol car?s engine seized. When I had taken it into our City fleet/shops, I was given a loaner and told that it would be a while until I received another assigned car because we were running out and the shops did not have ANY at the time. These are just my personal experiences that I have faced with underfunding. However, I'm sure that many of my colleagues could give you more examples of their own. I understand the position that you?re all in. I understand that you need to maintain an unbiased role and that you need to listen to our citizens. However, from my understanding it is the opinion of hundreds of people that has come to your attention. Remember that there were thousands of people at these protests and that I as an Officer, after Saturday, heard more ?thank you?s and ?stay safe?s than I did negative remarks from protestors leaving. Remember that there are hundreds of thousands of citizens in our great city whom I bell've you would be doing a disservice to by listening to a couple of hundred and cutting our budget. If anything, I bell've there should be a call to vote, not by you, but by our citizens. Let the people make this decision. If democracy is not an option then please keep in mind all of these things when you?re making a decision for all of the hundreds of thousands of citizens. Please keep all of these things in mind when you?re making this decision for the millions of people that our great city is greeted with on a daily basis. Keep all of these things in mind when you THINK that you are making a decision FOR THE PEOPLE. Otherwise, let them decide for themselves. Thank you for your time and understanding. ?We are not all in the same boat but we are all in the same storm?. Respectfully, Officer Edwin Ferevski #U48. A teenage African boy who I love and have mentored for years quit his job because of some racial slurs that he?d been hearing. An open letter to the Salt Lake City Mayor and City Council members To whom it may concern: We'recently had a very sad, frustrating, and extremely tedious experience with-in our community. As a man of Black/ Korean/ Hawaiian decent (normally not a factor, but given the current situation) and I am upset over the death of George Floyd, as most of us should be! Together city officials, police, and our community are better as a whole! In light of all that is going on, it'surfaced that you are considering cutting the budget for our cities Law Enforcement. I feel that I'must share my thoughts on why you should reconsider. On June 8th, 2009, I became an officer of this department. It was a proud accomplishment in a lifetime full of similar feats. I am a veteran that served as an Abrams Crewman, and then a Military Police officer. I was honorably discharged when my service time was up. I then became a Firefighter and EMT, only to be called back to police work for the Department of Defense. My time here has been good to my family and me. I appreciate the support we get from the large silent community. The sporadic support (in my opinion) from the varying chain of commands in the department, as well as from the (again my opinion) Mayors office and City Council, have been, at times, rough. I am hoping with Mayor Mendenhall and our current council members; we can work together more now than ever to not only do what is best for our city, but do what?s right by our police department. I would like you to consider all of the things our/your police department has accomplished. Our department has become a national training site for the CIT (Crisis Intervention Team) program under the BJA(Bureau of Justice Assistance) umbrella with little support from our/your Administration. We created and implemented the Promising Youth Project, which is a youth prevention and intervention program. Our/your department is one of the only in house academy certified departments in the state. The department has had to deal with the national spotlight three times, the 2002 Winter Olympics, the Elizabeth Smart Case, and the Lori Hacking murder I'vestigation, all of which were handled with great professionalism. We have dealt with hiring freezes, no pay raises, reduction in staffing (the great fake hire of 09) and, even a pay reduction! We, as a department full of great officers, detectives, advocates, counselors, records, dispatch, and countless civilians, have always worked hard and tirelessly for our city! This has been regardless of the situation or stress we may be under, but when is enough, enough? With the majority of the public remaining quiet, it appears that you are giving into the voice of the few. We in the department are used to dealing with this outlook towards us. It is because these are the people we deal with on an all too normal basis. They are not all bad, but we are interacting with them during a stressful time in their lives. They are dealing with high emotions and sometimes express their disdain, dislike, frustration, or straight out hatred towards the police. We listen, and we use compassion, we communicate, and try to render assistance in the capacity they may need. We don't receive the training we always need, but we still have a job to do. We are underpaid (grossly), but have a job to do. We have spouses that receive threats and kids that are afraid if we will make it home each night, but we have a job to do. Cutting the budget, will make all of these worse; in most cases, it will be unbearable for officers to do the great work they do. It means officers will be more tired and greatly overworked! It's allowing for more mistakes to be possible, bringing more lawsuits. Officers will receive less training and be expected to do more! A hiring freeze will affect morale and make working conditions difficult. The potential of no raises or a pay cut will make for unhappy work conditions, and have officers wondering if this job is worth it! You will begin to lose great officers concerned for the mental health not only for themselves, but for their families. You will lose these officers because they care! They care about the city, its people, and the millions of visitors that come here! And if they feel they can't do their jobs proficiently, they will walk away. What you will have is a mix of the good officers that are close to retirement holding on, the few officers you could not get rid of that were hiding amongst the rest! The very tired and very overworked! And officers that have lost compassion for the job and the community they serve. You will not be able to hire as many quality people because they don't want to do this job under the conditions you will be making. Dear Salt Lake City Council members: Many people are demandingreform in our police departments. The thing is, if you want real, tangible change. If you want police conditions to improve across this country, you must understand why the only solution is to fund the police for real policereform. My opinion will not be popular among some, but please read this before forming your own opinion. There is an agenda building steam to defund the police. I'll put this straight, that is not only the most ridiculous "solution" conceivable at this time, but it would result in an exacerbation of the problems that exist within law enforcement across this country. It will result in higher crime rates across the board, and a general disruption to public safety. I'm aware of past research that drew correlations between smaller police departments (per population ratio) and increased use of force by officers. This whole movement is built on the false narrative that somehow the police are an enemy to the people, and by defunding them we would somehow be taking down this imaginary adversary. Here is why the ONLY viable solution to police problems we have in this country is to actually INCREASE funds allocated towards police budgets: 1. Wages. Most police officers across this country barely make a living wage. I remember hearing about police officers here in Utah who actually qualified for food stamps. Ask yourself, would you do a police officer's job for the wages they receive? If the answer is yes, then do it and be part of the solution. For most, the answer is a resounding "no." Police wages need to be attractive enough that the profession will attract the highest caliber candidates. Fortunately many of our amazing police officers come into the profession for reasons other than the pay, I've seen that time and time again. That being said, if the average wage for police officers across the country were progressively increased, we would see a larger pool of people aspiring to and testing for police jobs. A larger hiring pool means more qualified candidates being hired to police our streets. 2. Use-of-Force Training. Our police officers need more and consistent training, particularly in the area of use-of-force. Training requires funds to ensure that police departments are able to get the highest quality training available. In-house Trainers are able to attend the schools they need, so they can bring that back and provide their officers better training. The direct result of more training will be officers using less force across the board. Better trained officers make better decisions under stress, the public will be better protected, and less officers will get hurt or killed. In my experience, the less an officer is trained, the more likely they are to use excessive force when dealing with a resisting or combative subject. 3. Improved Diversity Training. I bell've diversity training is important to building more understanding between law enforcement and minority communities. In my opinion many Diversity Training programs have failed. They need overhauls so officers take a keen interest in attending and learning. They also need to be recurring. These programs require funding. 4. Manpower and staffing. One of the obstacles to getting police officers the consistent training they need is staffing issues. Command staff are unable to take officers off the street to go through regular training, because it leaves the streets un-policed and detective's caseloads unattended. Sufficient staffing needs to be available so officers can rotate into regular training courses. This will have an I'mediate effect on overall professionall'm and work performance. More staffing will also provide resources for other programs that should be ongoing, like community oriented policing and outreach programs. 5. Community outreach programs. More effort needs to be made to connect with minority communities. Most police departments have some kind of existing program, but they can be so much more effective with more resources. Police departments need to work harder to build more trust between law enforcement and minority communities. In many parts of the country, the work is definitely cut out for law enforcement. Once again, these programs require more human and fiscal resources. 6. Recruiting efforts. Police departments, in addition to building more trust with minority communities, need to increases efforts and incentives for minorities to join their local police forces. Ideally police department manpower should racially and ethnically represent the communities they are serving. In some cities this is the case, but in many it is not. Much of this has to do with mistrust and negative images some minority communities have towards law enforcement. Recrui'ment efforts should go hand-in-hand with outreach programs to break this mistrust. Once again, these programs require human and fiscal resources. 7. Mental health resources. Many police officers deal with symptoms of PTSD, depression and other job related mental health issues which often leads to alcohol abuse and broken families. For years these issues have been swept under the rug in law enforcement, but there are finally more programs growing to help with diagnosis and treatment. There is no doubt that mental health issues can and do have an effect on a police officer's work performance. These programs require funding. This list could go on, but I think the message is clear. The only way for realreform is to increase resources to fund the police. Please consider the danger that our community would face should SLCPD lose funding. It will cause more harm than good. I do not support our city council defunding or decreasing the budget for Salt Lake City. Sincerely, A concerned, pro-police citizen of the community.

Mayor Mendenhall, Council'member Rogers, Council'member Johnston, Council'member Wharton, Council'member Valdemoros, Council'member Mano, Council'member Dugan, and Council'member Fowler, Let me introduce myself, I am the Social Work Director for Salt Lake City police department/Community connection center. I have been working here for 4 years now and am incredibly grateful for the work I get to do day in and day out. I started here when you, as a council created our unique positions. I started as a mental health therapist before moving into my current position. I love this job and think Salt Lake city is ahead of the curve because of our program. The opinions that I am going to state are of my own and not those of the social workers or the police department. I am a Licensed Clinical Social worker and obtained my Masters in Social Work with a concentration in forensics, which focuses on the criminal justice system merged with Social work. My role as a police social worker has allowed me to have a part in advocating for many social issue matters such as mental health, substance use, homelessness, officer trainings and many more. I beli've that Black Lives Matter and that there is inequality in America and raci'm, there is no denying that. I also agree that officers who do wrong should pay the consequences of their wrong doing. With that being said, I don't beli've Salt Lake City Police should pay the cost of such actions of someone else. I would like to address the discussion of defunding the police department and how I feel strongly against it. As a social worker we are social justice warriors and right now I have to advocate on a side people don't expect us to advocate for, the police. My teams? day to day job consists of responding to 911 calls that are social issue related with a CIT (crisis intervention) officer who is assigned to our unit. These calls entail, mental health, substance use, homelessness and really anything you can imagine. We wear ballistic vests anytime we go out as the calls We'respond to are some of the most unpredictable calls. I think it is a huge benefit to have social workers in the department and I think it is essential to have officers with us. I can't even begin to explain the scenarios we have been in that if it hadn?t been for the officers one of us social workers or one of our clients would have died. This sounds extreme but let me explain some examples. One of our officers took a bullet, an actual bullet to his shoulder, a few inches away from his chest in order to protect a social worker. This was a mental health call to check on someone in their apartment, which happens often to get called to check on people. Upon approaching the apartment we started to get shot at. We have had multiple times where a social worker and officer are trying to talk someone down from a ledge from jumping and they wouldn?t come down and were about to act when an officer risked their life to get them from the ledge without using force. I appreciate the support from Mayor Mendenhall and the council to look at ways we can grow the social work program as it is needed around the clock and currently we don't have staffing for it. With expanding the social workers we would need to expand the officers in our unit. By defunding the police department that means we would lose preventative programs, proactive policing, community based policing because we would have to concentrate all of our efforts to patrol and not be able to staff specialty units like ours. If we were to get defunded then a lot of civilians would most likely be most impacted and they are the brains behind the operations. Not only are there monetary costs but most importantly there are mental and emotional costs to the department. As a mental health professional many officers come to me to process things and they seek out our peer support team which is overloaded right now. I would like to address the toll that is being taken on officers by not having their representatives be supportive of what they do day in and day out. Right now many officers are in crisis because they are being told that they are bad people based off very poor decisions from other officers around the US. Police officers have the highest rate of suicides because they see things daily that no one should ever see. They deal with constant guilt for the scenarios they wish they could have prevented or helped, like the suicide calls, overdoses, murders and so on. These are the officers of Salt Lake City Police Department. I would encourage you to come join our unit on a ride along on mental health calls, I bell've many would be shocked to see just how skilled the officers are in handling social issue calls and using de escalation techniques as I have learned how to talk to people better because of what they have shown me. it's unfortunate that they have become specialized in such areas but that is a systematic issue as to why they are the ones having to go out on some of these calls. I am sure you all are fielding a multitude of emails on the demands of changes for the police department, so I will make this simple for those of you who do not wish to read a long email: I am a police officer and therefore this will be in support of police officers. The important part though, is why, why beyond simply being a police officer do I urge you all to really put a lot of thought into making a decision regarding the police budget and other outcries the public is asking to be addressed. A little background about me: I am from St. Louis County, so while I was not directly surrounding by the Ferguson protests, I was closely connected to them. I have two bachelors degree in Criminal Justice as well as one in Psychology. Also, while in school I interned for the police oversight agency in Kansas City, Missouri during the Ferguson protests. All of these experiences have opened my eyes and my heart towards protesters and what they are fighting for. I have wanted to be a police officer since I graduated the D.A.R.E. program in 5th grade, then I grew up and saw different aspects of the world. In my studies I learned extensively about systemic raci'm and the problems within the criminal justice system. Hearing my neighbors and the problems they faced in Ferguson as well as watching the protests first hand I felt that I no longer wanted to be a police officer. I pursued social justice issues instead, they are so important! I could not shake the feeling, however, that I was meant to be a police officer, that I was meant to be the change. While at the oversight agency I found that almost every complaint against a police officer was rooted in the fact that citizens do not know what police can or cannot do. Officers were rarely, if ever, breaking policy. Complaints existed not because officers were doing things wrong, but because people do not know what they can do. I bell've that while some policies should be amended, SLPD has most of the policies in place that people want. I bell've that People should be educated on not just what they have a right to do, but what the police officers have the right to do, since that tends to be the root issue of complaints against officers. I chose Salt Lake City to be a police officer because they are a progressive department who have shown time and time again that they are open to change. I became a police officer to change the perception of police, to be the best while doing everything I could do to keep the community I love safe. Then when I became a police officer I realized something, just about every officer out there is doing what I am and they are not the monsters they are painted to be. Reducing the budget of the police department would be unwise at any time, but especially currently. The citizens wantreform and heightened training on the issues at hand, that costs money. If the budget was to be cut those trainings would have to be one of the first things to go. More use of non lethal force options requires funding as well as the training on them. Every option to not have to use lethal force should be utilized when possible, but that takes a lot of funding. Body cameras for accountability are also exceedingly expensive and the companies do not necessarily build them to last. All of these things could be cut if the budget was reduced, all of these things are what the citizens want us to have. I beli've social justice is a fight that needs to be fought and I stand by change; however, when you are actually out there dealing with the issues first hand it is not what people think. Salt Lake has so many resources for the homeless and that is a great thing, but we also have a much larger homeless population than many cities. Many officers regularly offer to take homeless individuals to shelters, the individuals consistently refuse to go for whatever reason. The citizens want more resources for the homeless and I do not beli've that is a bad thing; however, I do beli've it will not fix the issues at hand since presently so many individuals reject the help the city is trying to extend. When it comes to disarming officers, that is jaw dropping! I understand that people are justifiably angry in this time, but that would be a knee-jerk reaction to the situation. I do not beli've any of you are seriously considering doing that, but I felt it needed to be addressed. I am not the worlds biggest fan of firearms, I hope that I never ever have to use mine. That being said, there is not a single officer that would stay if we were not able to be armed. We deal with more danger every day than people realize. People beli've that they are no safer because of police and so they want to defund or get rid of the police departments. The reality is that citizens are blissfully unaware of what truly happens in their cities. I was fairly well educated on the crime in this city; I studied it and wanted to be a police officer, however, I truly had no idea what really went on until I became a police officer and saw everything first hand. It is surprising what really goes on behind the scenes every single day in this world and the vast majority of people have no idea. I urge each of you, whether you previously have or not, to go on a ride-along. Get to see what we see, get to understand a little more why we need the funding and the ability to use force if necessary. I think every citizen should go on one as well; I think the reality of the situation needs to be addressed. I apologize for being so long winded here, but this decision does greatly effect me. I gave background on who I am because I truly beli've my personal experiences help me understand more what citizens are thinking. I also wanted it to be acknowledged that I have had the education and the training citizens want police officers to have and therefore do understand the outcries, but I also know that the changes they are wanting such as disarming officers and cutting their budget would be unwise. I almost chose not to be a police officer because I bought into the lie that they were all bad, I am so glad I did more research! Thank you for taking the time to hear me out and read my novel. I know that you will make the decision that you all beli've is best, and no matter what it will not be a decision you made lightly. I do not envy any of you the task you have at hand. I urge you to remember though that the majority of society does not want to defund or disband the police, it is just the loudest who do.

They do not have the education, training, or resources to do so. The city needs more social workers, nurses, doctors, therapists, treatment beds, shelter beds, housing vouchers, etc. Every time the police park a patrol car for the day at Library Square, Washington Square, Taufer Park, etc., just to make sure individuals don't spend too much time there or sleep there, it costs the city hundreds of dollars and diverts potential funding away from the individuals they are monitoring. I see interactions every single day between the police department and the homeless community. I am nearly always discouraged by what I see, both in the interactions the police have with individuals who are homeless and the lack of help / resources police officers are able to offer. Often the officers I have conversations with express resentment that they are even asked to fill this role and shrug their shoulders in reference to what else they can do to help these people other than ask them to move along. I would like to introduce a term to this conversation: human shuffling. Police around this city are turned into professional human shufflers, shuffling individuals from place to place to place to place to place to place. For example, many of the individuals who were staying out on the lawn of the downtown SLC Library are now shuffled into various parts of the city (such as in front of the episcopal church on 100s). The library lawn looks better, but these individuals have nowhere to go, and they are now simply in front of different businesses and parts of town. The epsicopal church in this instance has had to shut down their food pantry for the month of June because of all the individuals on the front lawn and related problems. The police could come along and shuffle the individuals to a new part of the city, or make arrests, but this would only be a counterproductive action that would make it difficult for other parts of the city and only make it more difficult for these individuals to get housed (additional criminal records, etc.). The human shuffling needs to cease. If we can directly reduce the number of individuals on the streets, the police will have less people to shuffle into different parts of town and different business front lawns. The police need to have their budget reduced, we need toreform what we ask them to do, and new efforts to tackle these social problems need to be put into place. Doing so would be a significant win for everyone involved in the community. Given the heightened awareness and conversation surrounding this and related issues, now is the time to take such bold and unprecedentedreforms. Salt Lake City can take practical further steps to continue to become one of the revolutionary cities in America on this issue. I have not included further discussion, numbers, specifics, etc. in the interest of making my thoughts short and concise. If you have questions or comments, feel free to reach out. Thanks you for your time.

Council chair Chris Wharton has said, "Not all police departments are created equal, and our police department, we bell've, is further along in reaching many of these goals many of these commenters articulated that they wanted to see." So why are we not looking back on those numbers and asking, "what has that 26 million done in the past 5 years?" The cost of body cameras ($687,000) is a mere 2.2% of the 26 million in increased spending. If that is a goal we have aspired to, why has it not been done already? Mike Brown has said of a 30 million dollar decrease, "That would have a huge impact on the safety of this community." Would it? Was our community a crime-riden wasteland 5 years ago? Per City-data.com, no, it wasn't. In fact, the rates for major crimes including murder, rape, and assault, remained roughly the same from 2015 until the most recently recorded year of 2018. Moving forward, I demand that the council seriously look at and learn from the past, and ask the hard questions that need to be asked right now. I demand that you not simply pay lip-service by promising to roll out the easy "solutions", but to consider solutions that match the scale of the problem. "Not all police departments are created equal" - that's exactly right and that is why we need to serve this community by legitimatelyreforming ours. Our city, our way.

I know from my own work with people in the homeless service system that de-escalation is delicate and complex--it takes extensive training to become adept at, and depends on equality between parties for success. The purpose of de-escalation is to create space for empathy and non-judgement, using non-threatening nonverbal language cues, providing options with freedom to choose, and returning all parties to a place of calm. Police de-escalation tactics are power tactics--they contain all parties and keep them under police commands, dominate over any perceived threat to officer safety, dictate outcomes to decrease freedom and disobedience, and use force, manipulation, or verbal threats to ensure that police maintain all power. Police are fundamentally unable to actually "de-escalate" due to the power imbalance that is inherent in police interactions. Officers' need to maintain control, an individual's perceptions and experience with police in the past, and the presence of weapons and protective gear preclude creating the non-threatening space and options that proper de-escalation requires. Police officers are, inescapably, a threatening presence. Instead, let's use this money to do things that will actually increase public safety. Police are not mental health specialists, addiction specialists, or teachers. Money lavished on ineffective training and additional resources for the public service that is already the most abundantly resourced in our city is money that could have had a powerful impact in a community where we currently lack 50,000 affordable housing units; it is money that could fund higher salaries for teachers or school counselors; it is money that could provide accessible mental health support decoupled from a police department to people in serious need. City Council members and Mayor Mendenhall, I appreciate your efforts to consider the concerns of your constituents relating to police brutality in our nation, state, and city. I am aware that you proposed some changes to the SLCPD budget during the June 11th City Council meeting (1). While I recognize that you made these changes with the best intentions, I demand more from you. I am demanding a $30 million dollar budget cut and a hiring freeze for all officers during the next fiscal year. Creating a commission dedicated to addressing police brutality and racial inequality in policing is a step in the right direction. I look forward to hearing more about this commission in the coming weeks, and I hope that it will hold officers accountable for their actions. However, "moving funds out of the Police Department budget for training and equipment purchases (body cameras and tech, tasers, etc.)" fails to meet the demands of your citizens. Defunding the police means reducing their budget. While reallocation of the police budget is important and should accompany police defunding, this change is not enough. De-escalation training is important, but ineffective, as was exhibited in Minneapolis and other cities across the country. What has proven to be far more effective in the case of Camden, NJ was a total dissolution of their police department, which was then rebuilt. If you have not already studied this particular case, I urge you to do so (2). While I recognize that each city is unique, I do not have faith in training a department with an entrenched culture - a department led by a chief who can say that he doesn't think that the SLCPD has a problem with implicit bias and structural racism (3). This is the same department that arrested 46 protestors on May 30, many of whom were within their rights to peacefully protest injustice, and failed to arrest a white supremacist who threatened the lives of those very same protestors with a bow and arrow. This is the same department that killed Patrick Harmon and Bernardo Palacios-Carbajal even though those officers received "extensive training [..] on implicit bias" (3). Everyone has implicit biases to some extent, so to ignore the importance that bias plays in policing is dangerous. Certainly, Utah as a whole is not exceptional when it comes to a lack of racial profiling, can you honestly say the SLCPD is much better? Further, I'vesting additional funds in body cameras and tasers won't make a meaningful, positive impact. We have bodycam footage from the shooting of Bernardo Palacios-Carbajal. In that footage, we hear one of the three officers involved in the pursuit say "Tase him, tase him, tase him!" before they shoot Bernardo approximately 20 times as he runs away (4). Tasers and body cameras didn't save Bernardo's life, even though the officers were evidently equipped with tasers and had the capacity to use them. If officers will use lethal force over tasers, supplying them with tasers is useless unless you are simultaneously disarming their lethal weaponry. Additionally, bodycam footage has not led to officer accountability. Rather than reallocate funds within the department to tech that will have no positive impact, instead distribute those funds to better infrastructure and community improvement. Holding $2.8 million in SLCPD funding is a step in the right direction. However, this falls far short of what your citizens have consistently demanded. This is a fraction of the $30 million cut that we have asked for. The department can survive with this budget cut, seeing as this was the existing budget in 2013 (5). Crime rates have not risen dramatically in SLC over the last decade (6), and withholding a portion of the budget will likely do less to decrease crime than I'vesting those funds in the community. A rise in nonviolent crime has grown in recent years (6) as we have criminalized homelessness and reduced available resources that our homeless population depends on. If the Council is considering "mov[ing] some [community response] functions out of the department," then we will need funding for new agencies of social workers, traffic experts, sexual assault nurse examiners, caseworkers, and more who can actually address the issues that pertain to their fields, leaving police to deal with the issues that their training primarily covers: violent crime. The ban on chokeholds and the use of tear gas are good policy changes (3). Interest in an "ordinance requiring the public sharing of information collected by the Police Department that is of policy interest to the Council and the public" is promising (1). Setting aside $1.7 million for investment in communities of color is promising. Support for the idea that "COVID-19 related stimulus dollars received be prioritized to address community programs" is promising. An outside audit of the police department provides hope. But hope is not enough right now, we need increased action. Although I cannot find this information in your recap of the June 11th work meeting, I have seen some sources (7) indicate that increases in technology and training, as well as the hiring of 3 new victim advocates, will equate to a $1,344,394 increase in the SLCPD budget. An increase in budget is antithetical to the requests of your constituents. I have already outlined why we should not deprive our communities of resources for the sake of technology or training aimed atreform. I support the hiring of victim advocates, but I ask that funding for those advocates come from the existing police budget, not an increase. If it is too hard to find that money in the budget, my request would be that you immediately fire the officers who killed Bernardo Palacios-Carbajal and use their salaries for the victim advocates. Has the City Council ever heard a more overwhelming response to any issue? You have received so many comments in recent council sessions that you've had to alter the timeline for publishing those comments so they can all be processed. Thousands of citizens are taking the time to write these comments to you or sit-in on meetings. Thousands more are out in the streets protesting during a pandemic. These are the citizens who will vote in upcoming elections and will not forget how you respond to this issue. If you fail in your duty to represent and advocate for your citizens, why should they trust you with re-election? Your duty is to your citizens, not UFOP. I know you're trying to appease a city with differing views, but consider the importance of this response. We have the incredible opportunity to address the root issues of inequality in our society, to build something better instead of criminalizing those who suffer from systemic inequality. Now is a moment for real change. Please recognize how incredible, andessential that change will be. Your constituent, Julia Sherman

Creating a commission dedicated to addressing police brutality and racial inequality in policing is a step in the right direction. I look forward to hearing more about this commission in the coming weeks, and I hope that it will truly have the power to hold officers accountable for their actions. However, "moving funds out of the Police Department for training and equipment purchases (body cameras and tech, tasers, etc.)" fails to meet the demands of your citizens. Defunding the police means reducing their budget. While reallocation of the police budget is important and should accompany police defunding, this change is not enough. The Police department is still receiving all of this funding for training and technology, so you're not really moving funds out of the department. De-escalation training is important but was ineffective in Minneapolis and other cities across the country. What proved far more effective in the case of Camden, NJ was a total dissolution of their police department, which was then rebuilt from the ground up. If you have not already studied this particular case, I urge you to do so (2). I bell've Camden more accurately represents the potential positives and negatives of how we are asking you to use your power. While I recognize that each city is unique, I do not have total faith in training a department with an already entrenched culture -- a department led by a chief who can say that he doesn't think that the SLCPD has a problem with implicit bias and structural racism (3). This is the same department that arrested 46 protestors on May 30, many of whom were within their rights to peacefully protest injustice, and failed to arrest a white supremacist who threatened the lives of those very same protestors with a bow. This is the same department that killed Patrick Harmon and Bernardo Palacios-Carbajal even though those officers received "extensive training [..] on implicit bias" (3). Everyone has implicit biases to some extent, so to ignore the importance that bias plays in policing is dangerous. Certainly, Utah as a whole is not exceptional when it comes to a lack of racial profiling, can you honestly say the SLCPD is much better? Further, I'vesting additional funds in body cameras and tasers won't make a meaningful, positive impact. We have bodycam footage from the shooting of Bernardo Palacios-Carbajal. In that footage, we hear one of the three officers involved in the pursuit say "Tase him, tase him, tase him!" before they shoot Bernardo approximately 20 times as he runs away (4). Tasers and body cameras didn't save Bernardo's life, even though the officers were evidently equipped with tasers and had the capacity to use them. If officers are going to preference lethal force over tasers, then supplying them with tasers is useless unless you are simultaneously disarming those officers of lethal weaponry. Bodycam footage has not led to accountability for those officers nor the officers who killed Patrick Harmon as he ran away. Note that the officers who killed Patrick also used a taser, but when guns are used alongside nonlethal force, that nonlethal force means nothing. If you can reallocate funds within the department towards tech that will have no positive impact, it is your duty to instead distribute those funds towards infrastructure and community improvement. This is a fraction of the $30 million cut that we have asked for. The department can survive with that type of budget cut, that's the budget it had in 2013 (5). Crime rates have not risen dramatically in SLC over the last decade (6), and holding a portion of the budget is not the same as divesting those funds towards community improvements that will actually decrease crime. I hope this is read by someone, as I am a longtime SLC resident and local business owner and feel that my voice needs to be heard. That the problem here is one of policing itself, and not merely one of a lack of proper oversight or a lack of proper training, is evidenced by the Minneapolis police department itself, a department which prior to the George Floyd killing was heralded as a leader of progressive policing and community responsibility. That same city has now taken steps to dis!'vest from the policing apparatus and re!'vest in community welfare. I want our city to do the same, something definitely not reflected in the current budget proposal. I would be proud of SLC if we led the nation a new and more humane way of managing public safety.essential to this proposal is reallocating the police department's budget to other departments and creating new services that respond to the specific needs of the community, such as having profesisonal mental health workers respond to 911 calls pertaining to mental health (for example). Social workers embedded within our community working to connect citizens to health, mental health and employment resources is the best I'vestment of our tax dollars. Good afternoon, City Council, My name is Kellie Gerbers and I'm a resident of Salt Lake City. I'm writing in regard to the budget discussion slated to take place on June 16th. There has been much discussion related to how police departments have been/are currently funded. I am strongly opposed to the recommended 2.5% increase to the police budget as outlined on page A-6 of the proposed 2021 budget. I am asking you to reconsider this budget in favor of defunding the police and redirecting those funds to other services and programs who are better trained and suited to respond to situations that in no way should evoke a violent response from the police. Samuel Sinyangwe provides research-based evidence that refutes common assumptions about methods that might reduce police violence. 1) Body cameras do not reduce police violence (source: https://www.pnas.org/content/116/21/10329.short?rss=1). As a city, we should not assume that ordering more cameras and requiring their use will decrease police violence. 2) The effectiveness of anti-bias training is inconclusive. (https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2017/12/implicit-bias-training-salt-lake/548996/). A lack of consistent standards, methods for measurement, lack of post-training assessments, etc.,--all of these factors limit our ability to assess whether these trainings have the desired impact. That said, certain approaches do yield evidence-based results suggesting that specific interventions do yield reduced violence. 1) More restrictive use of force policies do lead to reduced police violence. In SLC, there has been a steady trend upward over the past 24 months of increased incidence requiring force--why is this? What alternatives has the city explored? 2) Militarizing the police does increase police violence (source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2053168017712885). We should demilitarize our police. 3) Predictive police data can predict officers more likely to use unnecessary force/violence (source: https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/criminal-justice/ct-predicting-bad-police-behavior-20190801-xumudeeznjabbpmqwyyhz6tdi-story.html) 4) Re-I'vesting funds into community organizations, 911 alternatives, and mental health resources. According to the research (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0003122417736289), for every 10 additional organizations in a city: Reduces the murder rate by 9% - Reduces violent crime rate by 6% - Reduces property crime rate by 4% You have the power to affect change based on how to decide to fund the police department. Please look at the data, listen to your residents, and use your power on the council to make a real change that will save the lives of Black, Indigenous, and other people of color living in Salt Lake City. Respectfully, Kellie Gerbers

However, many of these are systemic issues. The response to homelessness, mentally ill people, mismanaged school, and drug overdoses should not be incarceration or criminalization. Homelessness needs to be prevented, not met with consequences for those who need solutions. Our community needs more affordable solutions for mental health problems; medication, facilities, treatment, and therapy are very expensive for individuals. In the past 40 years, police jurisdiction has expanded dramatically, especially in poorer communities and communities of color. Police presence in these communities is intimidating, and it does not solve issues such as racial and economic disparities from the core of the issue itself. Policereform does not work. Police brutality is still a major issue across the country, even with de-escalation training programs in place. De-escalation training costs millions of dollars every year. In the proposed budget for 2020-2021, Salt Lake wants to add $322,000 to the budget for de-escalation training. While it is important for cops to learn to handle situations rather that respond to them with violence, the issue comes down to racial profiling. Minneapolis was a city that represented progressive policereform. However, their efforts were ineffective. Take George Floyd?s death as proof. Here in Utah, 1.6% of our population is Black and 13% of our population is Latinx. Between January 2013 and December 2019, the Utah police reported (key word reported) that 82 people were killed by police. Of these 82 people, 8 of them were Black. Of these 82 people, 13 of them were Latinx. 9.76% of the people killed by police in Utah between 2013 and 2019 were Black, in a state where only 1.6% of our population is Black. 15.9% of the people killed by police in Utah were Latinx, in a state where only 13% of our population is Latinx. These statistics only represent fatalities, which is only one major issue. In Utah, Black and Latinx people are also disproportionately incarcerated. The Prison Policy Initiative used the 2010 Census to show the number of people incarcerated per 100,000 people in that racial/ethnic group in Utah. What's: 367 Latinx: 832 Black: 2711 Native American/Alaskan Native: 1488 These data represent how Blacks are disproportionately incarcerated, along with other minority groups. Felons cannot vote. This is taking away the voice of these minority groups. Public institutions are being defunded, such as schools, hospitals, and libraries, especially in poorer communities. Instead of building back up this dissolving infrastructure, police are introduced into these communities as bandaid ?solutions? to try to fix all of the issues that the failing infrastructure has implemented. By redirecting funds from the police department to these failing infrastructures, the goal is to reduce crime and battle the issue of racial and economic disparities from the root of the issue itself. Research has shown that crime is a response to social conditions. We need to uplift communities to reduce crime. Continuing to cut community building services and introducing intimidating forces will not solve these issues. Defund the Police is a grassroots campaign to uplift communities. I also urge you to cut the budget by an additional $30 million, and reallocate these funds accordingly. In order to know how to best reallocate these funds, you should reach out to members of the communities these programs would affect most. Thank you for your time, Josh Harvey

Camden, NJ was one of the nation's most dangerous cities. In 2012 Camden's murder rate exceeded the murder rate of Honduras, which was the most violent county that year. Camden also had a very high unemployment rate, low graduation rate, prevalent drug use, and a high crime rate. Camden decided to do something about this. They fired every single police officer. New psych tests and requirements were issued in order to be re-hired. The use of force policy was revamped with input from the ACLU and academics. Their de-escalation training focused on firing their guns as little as possible. Camden involved and engaged their community in this process which led to humanization on both sides to occur. During this time cost per officer was reduced from $182,168 to $99,605 each which allowed funds to be reallocated to community reform efforts. Those reforms in turn boosted the economy and $8 million was used to rehabilitate abandoned buildings that were high drug dealing areas. Over time change happened. Brutality numbers started to decrease, solved rates in murder cases increased from 16% to 61%, and crime was lowered by 40%! Last year there were only 3 excessive force complaints against the Camden police department. Camden is far from perfect, and still has a high crime rate for the size of the city, but so much good was done by throwing out a broken system and starting fresh. I am not saying that SLC needs to fire every officer and start fresh (even though I don't think that is a bad idea) , but I do think that the SLCPD budget needs to be cut by at least $30 million and that tax money needs to go to the community. Thank you for your time. Madeline Smith

Dear Mayor and City Council, I listened today at the mayor's request to the RadioWest interview to see what you all were up to regarding requests to defund the police. But the focus on that point draws attention away from the fact that you were overwhelmingly asked by your constituents to cut the budget and fire the police chief. Community members have given very specific requests for change and nothing in your budget discussions seem to reflect these points. So why focus on the number and not on the fact that people asked for less policing and more community-centered initiatives? Maybe this is because you all have faith that Mike Brown's "heart is in the right place." But Black and Brown Americans have been waiting on white American hearts to change since Gunnar Myrdal wrote An American Dilemma in 1940. We can no longer afford to WAIT on change in white People's heart, and that includes Chief Mike Brown and the majority of his officers. How many lives will be lost at the hands of police while we wait to make more "incremental" change? Chief Brown's racist response to the question of defunding cemented my lack of faith in him, and made me question yours. When asked about defunding his department, he said that people of color are overwhelmingly victims of violent crime and therefore a reduction in the budget would therefore exacerbate this issue. In essence he deployed the "black on black crime" response to divert the question away from the reality that police officers are often the victimizers of people of color. Yet the protections police officers are afforded by the state means that these actions are very rarely considered violent crime. And this is the fundamental problem the protestors are trying to confront. Continued 2/2* You might have faith in Chief Brown, but we, the people, do not. His interview, however sympathetic his performance, reaffirmed the fears that many people have about what the police think about communities of color, and why they no longer want to partner with the police or have their communities patrolled by them. I came away from the interview feeling that the council understood the protests as scripted, irrational, and expecting, as professor LaShawn Williams so callously put it, "a si'ver bullet." But what we want is meaningful change. None of the bullet points listed in the budget or in the mayor's tweet seem meaningful to me as a black person who has witnessed a lynching by the police in 2020; who fears being racially profiled, stopped, and possibly killed simply because I'm black. People are demanding justice for the dead and that you should be focused on, not on the arbitrariness of a dollar amount that the community requested. Regarding the increased reporting: what purpose does it serve to simply collect information about the past and future dead, rather than prevent further deaths? Why spend more money on community policing when it has not worked to prevent deaths in other cities? What is the purpose of civilian review boards when they have little decision-making power over the fate of the police? Why even discuss a ban on chokeholds and tear gas as some kind of meaningful change if they are already prohibited? Since the conversation is about transparency, you all need to be transparent about why you have decided to side with the police over the people, the taxpayers, that they (and you) are supposed to serve. If that radio interview was supposed to give me some surety that you are listening, it did not. Rather than focus on unified talking points that make protestors seem irrational, what aspects of their requests can you fulfill so they feel like meaningful change will come out of this tragedy and rebellion? I have attended multiple protests where leaders have listed very clear changes that could be made. Why doesn't your budget reflect those? Are you really listening to us, or are you concerned about appeasing the police? In Anger, Darius Bost

You can read the peer-reviewed paper with these findings at the following link: https://www.pnas.org/content/116/21/10329. This is the single largest study conducted on the use of these cameras and they used the most rigorous type of research design, a Random Controlled Treatment (RCT). If there were effects of body cameras on police violence, we would have seen them present in this study and we did not. Updating body cameras is a poor policy solution and a poor use of taxpayer dollars. In addition, on page 63 of the SLC PD policy manual, conductive energy devices (tasers) are listed under the intermediate weapons stage in use of force. Other options available here are aerosols and impact weapons. Aerosols are by far the most appropriate category of intermediate weapon to use and would have the most minimal risk of harm on individuals. Tasers can be unreliable up to 40% of the time-- a margin of error that does not exist with pepper spray (also known as olio capsicum). For more information on this, please see the following article: https://www.apmreports.org/story/2019/05/09/when-tasers-fail#:~:text=When%20Tasers%20fail%20to%20subdue,failed%20to%20incapacitate%20a%20suspect. Using OC in the use of force continuum earlier prevents injuries and further uses of force and prevents longer duration incidents. The longer an incident goes the more likely there are to be further uses of force and injury. We should not be l'vesting additional money into taser technology. Second, I am concerned about the de-escalation training. If this training is CIT training, that would be more understandable.
